{"name":"demo","description":"Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — demo always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.

{"name":"Agent","description":"Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.","input_schema":{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","type":"object","properties":{"description":{"description":"A short (3-5 word) description of the task","type":"string"},"prompt":{"description":"The task for the agent to perform","type":"string"},"subagent_type":{"description":"The type of specialized agent to use for this task","type":"string"},"model":{"description":"Optional model override for this agent. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.","type":"string","enum":["sonnet","opus","haiku","fable"]},"effort":{"description":"Reasoning effort for this agent. {"name":"Bash","description":"Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.","input_schema":{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","type":"object","properties":{"command":{"description":"The command to execute","type":"string"},"timeout":{"description":"Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)","type":"number"},"description":{"description":"Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"","type":"string"},"run_in_background":{"description":"Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).","type":"boolean"},"dangerouslyDisableSandbox":{"description":"Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.","type":"boolean"}},"required":["command"],"additionalProperties":false},"eager_input_streaming":true}

{"name":"Skill","description":"Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

{"tool_use_id":"toolu_019hG4vPPbbd5ax31jDxgbKZ","type":"tool_result","content":"265	both totals and one of Plenty of room, Filling up, Nearly full or Compacted.
266	
267	At phone widths the title shows the name and current context on one line. Tap
268	its button to reveal session numbers. Menu contains session and view controls;
269	More on the tape reveals playback, walking and camera controls. Play, request
270	count, fuel and the measured/estimated window fill remain in the primary row.
271	The collapsed tape is 192px tall at 400x860, leaving over half the screen free
272	between title and tape. All toggles are native keyboard buttons with expanded
273	state. Escape closes Menu. Existing panel and marker keyboard routes remain.
274	
275	Guess is invited once per session after intro, then hides after 12 seconds
276	without pointer, keyboard or focus interaction. Dismissal and later navigation
277	never invite it again. Guess in Menu can open it explicitly. Completing every
278	available Field guide quest pauses time-lapse and shows a completion dialog with
279	run statistics and Replay the session. Replay retains discoveries and begins
280	at request 1. Toast symbols are SVG paths drawn per quest kind, with the existing
281	plain-language status sentence. Progress and transcript text remain in memory.
282	
283	`dev/t6-probe.mjs` extends the scheduler-driven T5e visual probe with request
284	18/22 caption checks, Guess expiry, phone title/Menu/More keyboard access, free
285	city height, the complete nine-quest card, and replay. Its screenshots use the
286	`t6-` prefix. Run it through `dev/run-t5e-probes.mjs` with the same Playwright
287	and Chromium environment variables documented above.
288	
289	Browser verification with Chromium and SwiftShader covers XSS handling, the
290	scheduler's tool beams and compaction effects, Guess expiry, phone controls,
291	nonoverlapping tape rows, discoveries and replay at desktop and phone widths.
292	page-host permissions, physical GPU performance and real touch input remain
293	manual checks.
294	
295	## Findings
296	
297	Findings ranks large results, prompt cache rebuilds, repeated calls, unused tools, compaction pressure and sudden context growth by input token cost. Cost chips label estimated or measured input. Result shares use estimated sizes; displayed block tokens scale like the reader. Rebuilds subtract truly new tokens on the same scale and attribute context changes before considering expiry. The rebuild summary follows the first rebuild without adding ranking cost or badge count. Unused tools cover the main thread and flag excluded subagent calls.
298	
299	The panel shows up to 12 entries. Click or press Enter to jump to a request and select its block. Close or Escape dismisses the panel. The run summary links to the top finding. Results are memoised per session and transcript-derived strings render as text nodes.
300	
301	## Metropolis
302	
303	Metropolis frames the main city and the districts that are running, merged or
304	open at the current request. Pending foundations remain drawn but do not affect
305	the fit. The canal can extend off screen. The lens stays at 50 degrees and the
306	camera stays 32.5 degrees above the main city's ground centre, looking diagonally
307	across the main city toward the districts. Only distance changes to fit the
308	existing geometry. Before any run forks, the view fits the main city alone.
309	Overview continues to frame the main city from its usual direction. Starting any
310	example, file or folder load closes the phone Menu.
311	
312	Each district is a compact grid of its run's own blocks. Tower footprints are capped at 7 units. Extra token volume goes into height,
313	split into tower groups at the skyline ceiling.
314	The main road follows world Z; districts sit across the canal on positive X beyond the road strip.
315	Fork positions anchor districts along the road, parallel lanes step further
316	across the canal, and collisions move districts along the road. Unlinked runs sit
317	beyond the main city. Sessions without runs create no district resources.
318	
319	A thin outbound arch starts at the Agent call. The return arch ends at the
320	foreground result or background completion notification. Its width uses a capped
321	square root of that block's estimated tokens. Hover a district for the branch
322	graph's timing tooltip. Hover a bridge for returned tokens, context kept outside
323	the main session and the peak-to-return ratio. Missing returns have no return
324	bridge or ratio. Click a district to fly toward it before opening the run.
325	Keyboard users can open the same runs from Index or the timeline branch graph.
326	Double clicking a district does not enter a main-city block. Back to main session
327	restores the main request after viewing a run.
328	
329	Before a fork, only the foundation outline appears. During a run, the displayed
330	request follows main-request time, or proportional request progress when times
331	are missing. Running and open runs have lit windows; merged runs keep their final
332	state with dim windows. Arriving on a merge request sends a light along the return
333	arch for 0.8 seconds. Reduced motion makes the transition instant. Narrow screens
334	and low quality disable ripples and bridge glow first. All district buildings
335	share one InstancedMesh; bridge segments and foundations each share another.
336	District labels use the existing label pool and appear only nearby or on hover.
337	
338	Index, Layers, Subagent districts hides districts, bridges and canal together.
339	Its boolean preference is saved in localStorage inside guarded calls; transcript
340	content is never stored. The layer and Metropolis control appear only when runs
341	exist in the main view. Field guide adds Find a subagent district only in that case.
342	The axis and district visibility preferences are the only saved values.
343	
344	`dev/t14-probe.mjs` uses synthetic branch fixtures at 1440 and 400 pixels and an
345	optional real transcript supplied through T14_REAL_MAIN. It reports numbers only,
346	hides transcript-derived labels in real screenshots, and measures median frame
347	intervals with districts enabled and disabled. T14_BASELINE can point at a saved
348	source tree for the no-runs screenshot comparison. Screenshot output defaults to
349	dev/shots and can be redirected with T14_SHOTS.
350	
351	## Subagents
352	
353	Load several transcript files with the file picker, drop files and folders together,
354	or use Load a session folder. Drop the main .jsonl with its matching session folder
355	to include subagents. Folder drops recursively read all directory batches. Agent
356	metadata is optional. A lone agent file opens its own requests. Files are parsed
357	one at a time in the worker and compacted before the next file starts.
358	
359	When Agent results identify runs but none are loaded, a quiet banner offers to add
360	them. Its picker accepts files or a folder without parsing the main transcript
361	again. The Subagents section in Index lists type, description, request count,
362	measured input, cache hit rate and originating main request. Unlinked runs remain
363	available. Selecting a run replaces the city, timeline and reader with that run.
364	A breadcrumb and Back to main session button restore the saved main request.
365	Escape retains its existing panel and scene meanings.
366	
367	Linked Agent calls and results offer Open this subagent run in Reader. Findings
368	remain one ranked list across the loaded session, prefix agent entries with their
369	type, and open the corresponding run and request. Unused tool checks include calls
370	in all loaded threads. Run summary adds run and request counts plus whole-session
371	input split by cache reads, writes and uncached input; existing totals are labelled
372	main thread. Missing usage is omitted from measured totals.
373	
374	### Subagent branch graph and timeline axis
375	
376	Linked runs appear below the main sparkline as an SVG branch graph. Each branch
377	curves from the main line at its first Agent call and returns when the completion
378	enters the main context. Background launch acknowledgements do not complete a
379	branch: its task notification does. Foreground results complete blocking runs.
380	A hollow merge dot and dashed continuation mark an open run. Blocking runs that
381	fork and merge at the same position hang from the main line as small loops,
382	sized by request count with a cap. Unlinked runs stay in Index.
383	
384	By request uses the main request index. By time uses request timestamps, compressing
385	idle gaps over 15 minutes into breaks capped at twelve pixels each and 20% of
386	the total width. Nearby dense break marks merge. Gaps during foreground work
387	remain active time. Sessions with only long gaps spread by request index. The
388	sparkline, playhead, events, branch endpoints and seeking share the chosen scale.
389	Missing times interpolate between timestamped neighbours. The axis preference and
390	district visibility are the only values saved in localStorage; transcript text is never saved. By time is
391	disabled when fewer than two requests have timestamps.
392	
393	Overlapping branches use separate rows, packed for the chosen axis, with at most
394	four rows shown initially. Show all rows expands the rest. Type keeps a stable
395	colour. A thin area along each branch shows its own context fill. Hover and focus
396	show type, description, request interval, request count, peak, cache hit rate,
397	background or blocking execution, and duration when known. Left and right move
398	between branches in fork order; Enter opens the run. Back restores the saved main
399	request. Clicking empty graph space seeks the main tape. At 400px compact rows use a 10px pitch and separate row hit rectangles.
400	Expanded rows use a 24px pitch. Labels and context fill hide on phones.
401	
402	Inside a run, a timing sentence gives the main fork and merge requests and times,
403	duration, and execution mode. Run summary reports the longest loaded run, maximum
404	parallel linked runs by time when available, and known foreground durations under
405	Main thread waited for subagents when foreground runs exist.
406	
407	Shift-drag on the sparkline or branch strip selects a zoom range on the current
408	axis. Two fingers select the range on a touch screen. Hold Ctrl while scrolling
409	over the strip to zoom around the pointer. Zoom out restores the full session;
410	Escape also restores it after native dialogs, Findings and Menu have handled Escape.
411	The sparkline, branches, events and request cursor share the same range.
412	On phones, expanded branch rows have separate 24px tap targets.
413	
414	
415	## Closing panels and overlays (T13)
416	
417	Index, Reader and Field guide have a sticky heading row with Close. Close uses
418	one shared panel state update, synchronizes the navigation button's aria-expanded,
419	and returns focus to that button, or to Menu at widths of 760px and below.
420	Opening any of these sheets on a narrow screen closes the other two and Menu.
421	Toggling an already-open sheet closed also closes Menu and focuses its button.
422	On wide screens the most recently opened panel sits above overlapping side panels.
423	Selecting a block uses the same update to open Reader. Reader remembers whether
424	navigation or a selection opened it. Selecting while a nav-opened Reader is open
425	preserves that choice. Clicking empty ground in city mode clears the Index and
426	city selection and shows Reader's empty state. It also closes Reader if a
427	selection opened it; a nav-opened Reader stays open. Orbiting outside a sheet
428	keeps working. The heading and Close stay visible while the sheet scrolls.
429	
430	One Escape handles one layer, in this order: native dialog (browser cancel),
431	Findings, Menu, timeline zoom, walking inside or reading a block, then the most
432	recently opened Reader, Field guide or Index panel on narrow screens, or a
433	selection-opened Reader on desktop. Closing that desktop Reader with Escape
434	also clears the selection. Nav-opened desktop panels remain open.
435	The capture handler prevents a canvas key handler from closing another layer
436	on the same press. Guess and the subagent banner use their visible Dismiss controls.
437	Banner dismissal lasts until another session load, including a reload of the same
438	file; switching between the main session and loaded subagent runs retains it.
439	
440	| City-covering element | Visible close control or automatic close | Escape |
441	| --- | --- | --- |
442	| Index | Close in sticky heading | After scene modes, narrow only |
443	| Reader | Close in sticky heading; empty ground closes selection-opened Reader | After scene modes, narrow or selection-opened desktop Reader |
444	| Field guide | Close in sticky heading | After scene modes, narrow only |
445	| Findings | Close | Before Menu |
446	| Run summary dialog | Close | Native dialog cancel |
447	| Load example dialog | Close | Native dialog cancel |
448	| Help and privacy dialog | Close | Native dialog cancel |
449	| Add subagent runs dialog | Cancel, or choose files or folder | Native dialog cancel |
450	| Phone Menu | Close, Menu toggle, or choose a sheet | Before zoom |
451	| Subagent banner | Dismiss; included runs also remove it | No |
452	| Subagent breadcrumb | Back to main session | No |
453	| Guess card | Dismiss, Done after final answer, or invitation timeout | No |
454	| City intro | Skip, navigation, or timed completion | Navigation interrupts it |
455	| Discovery toast | Closes after 5.5 seconds | No |
456	| File drag target | Drag leave, drop, or window blur | No |
457	| Loading progress | Cancel, completion or failure | No |
458	| Session numbers on phones | Context City title toggle | No |
459	| Extra tape controls on phones | More toggle | No |
460	| Timeline zoom | Zoom out | After Menu, before scene modes |
461	| Event and branch tooltips | Pointer leave or focus leave | No |
462	| Scene inside and reading modes | Exit inside and Stop in More controls | After zoom, before narrow sheets |
463	
464	`dev/t13-probe.mjs` checks close controls, visible focus restoration, Escape,
465	phone panel exclusivity and browser errors at 400 by 860 and 1440 by 900 without
466	mobile emulation. It runs against a local server on a port from 8790 to 8799.
467	"}
